picks.title: Multi-omics insights into rare earth element recovery by microalgae under salinity gradients.
picks.hook: Microalgae pull valuable rare earths from salty water, offering a greener extraction route.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to understand how tiny green algae can pull rare earth elements out of water, especially when the water’s salt level changes. 

The researchers grew a microalga in laboratory cultures and exposed it to different salinity conditions, then used a suite of molecular techniques that together examine genes, proteins and metabolites – a “multi‑omics” approach – to see what was happening inside the cells. 

They found that the algae’s ability to recover rare earth metals was strongly affected by the salt concentration, and that specific molecular pathways were switched on or off depending on the salinity level. 

These insights suggest that tweaking the salt environment could make algal rare‑earth recovery more efficient, offering a greener alternative to traditional extraction methods.
picks.why: Understanding salt‑driven mechanisms can help develop sustainable algae‑based processes for extracting valuable metals.

picks.title: Start‑up and functional performance assessment of electron-shuttling-driven microalgal-anammox process.
picks.hook: Electron‑shuttling microbes boost a microalgal‑anammox system for low‑energy nitrogen removal.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to see whether a partnership between a microalga and anammox bacteria could speed up the start‑up of the anammox process, which is prized for its low energy use and strong nitrogen removal but is usually slow to begin working.

The researchers built a symbiotic system using the green microalga Chlorella vulgaris together with anammox bacteria, and they tested its performance in a laboratory‑scale reactor, monitoring how quickly nitrogen and phosphorus were removed.

The results showed that the microalgal‑anammox system reduced the start‑up time and achieved removal of nitrogen and phosphorus, although the abstract does not give specific percentages or rates.

This is interesting because shortening the start‑up period could make anammox‑based wastewater treatments more practical and cost‑effective.
picks.why: Faster start‑up of anammox with algae could help bring low‑energy nitrogen removal to real‑world wastewater plants.

picks.title: DnaK1-mediated regulation of phototactic motility in Synechococcus elongatus UTEX 3055.
picks.hook: DnaK1 controls light‑driven swimming in Synechococcus, revealing new phototaxis engineering targets.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to discover how light signals control the swimming direction of the cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus UTEX 3055. The researchers focused on a protein called DnaK1, which they suspected might link light detection to the cell’s motility machinery.

They examined the role of DnaK1 by creating mutants that lack the dnaK1 gene and by testing interactions with known phototaxis regulators, such as the type IV pilus (T4P) motor component PilB and the phototaxis regulator PixG. The work was done on laboratory cultures of the bacterium using molecular genetics and motility assays.

The study found that DnaK1 interacts with PixG and the T4P extension ATPase PilB, and that loss of dnaK1 impairs phototactic motility. Mutations in dnaJ1, another related chaperone, were also examined, indicating a broader chaperone network influencing movement.

These findings clarify a missing link in how cyanobacteria translate light cues into directed swimming, which could help engineer light‑responsive microbial systems.
picks.why: Understanding DnaK1’s role in light‑driven movement may enable better design of algae for bio‑production or environmental monitoring.

picks.title: Treatment of synthetic acid mine drainage (AMD) by photoautotrophic and mixotrophic cultivation of Galdieria sulphuraria.
picks.hook: Galdieria sulphuraria cleans synthetic acid mine runoff, turning toxic water into biomass.
picks.article:
A recent study explored whether the extremophile alga Galdieria sulphuraria could be used to clean up synthetic acid mine drainage, a highly acidic, metal‑rich wastewater generated by mining and related industries. 

The researchers cultivated the alga in laboratory flasks containing synthetic AMD, testing both photoautotrophic conditions (using only light and CO₂) and mixotrophic conditions (adding an organic carbon source). 

The results suggested that Galdieria sulphuraria grew well in synthetic AMD under both cultivation modes. 

This finding is interesting because it points to a potentially low‑impact, biological way to treat acidic, metal‑laden waste streams.
picks.why: Algal growth in acid mine drainage could offer a greener method for metal removal and water remediation.
